core: Working definition of evidence-based public health: using the best available research and data to guide decisions (attributed to CDC)
Three kinds of evidence: surveillance data, studies, and program evaluations
Study types: cohort studies, case-control studies, randomized trials
The evidence hierarchy idea, with the honest caveat that good questions matter more than rank
What evidence can and cannot do: it informs decisions but does not make them alone
The connection between evidence and policy (public-health-policy is a sibling topic)
supporting: The Community Guide and CPSTF as the evidence-review machinery of U.S. public health
CDC surveillance as continued watchfulness over disease trends
The flashlight-not-map framing as the honest reality check
outOfScope: Epidemiology methods in depth (sibling topic: epidemiology)
Risk concepts and measures (sibling topic: risk)
How laws and policies are made, enforced, or challenged (sibling topic: public-health-policy)
Clinical evidence-based medicine as a separate discipline

claims.claim: Evidence-based public health is the practice of using the best available research and data to guide decisions about programs, policies, and services.

CDC describes evidence-based practice in terms of choosing evidence-based programs and policies, and its gateway pages compile the resources, such as ACIP recommendations and The Community Guide, that decision makers use.

The Community Preventive Services Task Force (CPSTF) makes evidence-based recommendations about the effectiveness and economic impact of public health programs, services, and interventions used in real-world settings, and its findings make up The Community Guide.
Surveillance data are evidence: public health surveillance is the systematic, continuous collection and evaluation of health information to watch the distribution and trends of disease over time.
Studies are evidence: epidemiologic studies compare groups of people to test whether exposures are associated with health outcomes.
A cohort study records whether each participant is exposed or not, then follows the participants over time and compares disease rates between the exposed and unexposed groups.
A case-control study starts by enrolling people with the disease and a comparison group without it, then compares the two groups' past exposures.

In an experimental study or randomized trial, the investigator determines the exposure through a controlled process, such as randomly assigning persons to treatment or comparison groups, and tracks the effects.

Some study designs provide stronger evidence than others: CDC's own teaching notes that a cross-sectional study is analytically weaker than a cohort or case-control study, and randomized trials are generally regarded as the strongest design.
Evidence informs decisions but does not make them alone: the evidence-review process weighs effectiveness and economic impact, and communities add values, resources, and preferences when they choose.

Data guide policy choices: CDC publishes guidelines and recommendations to help decision makers choose courses of action, and The Community Guide's evidence-based findings inform decisions about programs, services, and policies at the community level.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether evidence should decide policy or merely inform it.
positions: Evidence-based practice can be read as 'the data decide', which would leave no room for values, budgets, or community preferences.
The evidence-review bodies themselves weigh effectiveness alongside economic impact and issue recommendations, leaving the final choice to decision makers.
Critics note that 'evidence-based' language can be used to disguise value judgments as science.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the honest middle position: evidence is necessary and powerful but not sufficient; it informs and constrains decisions without making them alone. This matches how CPSTF recommendations (effectiveness plus economic impact, real-world settings) are actually used.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How strictly the evidence hierarchy should be applied.
positions: Some presentations rank designs rigidly, implying randomized trials always beat observational studies.
CDC notes that different designs answer different questions and that a cross-sectional study is a fine tool for descriptive purposes, only weaker analytically.
Methodologists caution that a well-conducted observational study can be more reliable than a poorly conducted trial.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the hierarchy simply (some studies are stronger than others, trials generally at the top) with the honest caveat that the question asked matters more than the rank of the design.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's boilerplate ('a foundational concept in Public Health', 'College courses use evidence in public health as a building block') carried no factual content and was discarded.
The draft's generic vocabulary ('context', 'application') was replaced with field-accurate terms (cohort study, case-control study, surveillance data, program evaluation, evidence hierarchy).
The draft's 'toolbox drawer label' analogy was replaced with the flashlight-not-map framing required by the topic brief.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced all generic draft prose with a source-verified lesson on evidence-based public health.
Attributed the working definition to CDC and supported it with the CDC evidence-based practices gateway page and the CPSTF About page.
Added one-line treatments of the three evidence types and three study types, each supported by CDC Principles of Epidemiology.
Stated the evidence hierarchy with the honest caveat (good questions matter more than rank), grounded in CDC's own note that cross-sectional studies are analytically weaker.
Confirmed the evidence-and-policy connection with CDC guidelines/recommendations language and The Community Guide's purpose, keeping policy mechanics in the sibling topic public-health-policy.

sourceRecords.title: About The Community Guide
sourceRecords.provider: The Community Guide (Community Preventive Services Task Force, supported by CDC)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly (thecommunityguide.org is reachable). The Community Guide is a collection of evidence-based recommendations and findings from the CPSTF; CPSTF makes evidence-based recommendations about the effectiveness and economic impact of programs, services, and interventions in real-world settings; recommendations are described as the gold standard for what works to protect and improve population health. Supports the evidence-and-policy and informs-not-decides claims.

sourceRecords.title: About the Community Preventive Services Task Force (CPSTF)
sourceRecords.provider: The Community Guide (Community Preventive Services Task Force, supported by CDC)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly. CPSTF, established in 1996 by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, develops guidance on which community-based intervention approaches work and which do not, based on available scientific evidence; its recommendations and findings are based on systematic reviews of evidence of effectiveness and economic impact; members are appointed by the CDC director and CDC's Community Guide Program provides scientific support. Supports the working-definition and informs-not-decides claims.
